3A.question: Whether the language has many more consonants than vowels, or a more balanced mix.
3A.mt_relevance: A phonology-level trait that mostly matters for romanization and speech; consonant-heavy words also tend to fragment more under subword tokenizers.

4A.question: Whether the language distinguishes voiced from voiceless sounds, like 'b' versus 'p'.
4A.mt_relevance: Mainly a speech and transliteration issue; when a script under-marks voicing, distinct words can collapse into a single romanized spelling.

5A.question: Which basic stop consonants (like p, t, k, b, d, g) the language's sound system lacks.
5A.mt_relevance: Mostly shapes how loanwords are respelled: a missing /p/ or /g/ forces borrowed names into substitute letters, tripping up transliteration.

6A.question: Whether the language has uvular consonants — 'throaty' sounds far back in the mouth.
6A.mt_relevance: Chiefly a transliteration concern: uvular sounds map unevenly to Latin letters (q, gh, kh), scattering one name across several spellings.

7A.question: Whether the language has glottalized consonants like ejectives or implosives.
7A.mt_relevance: These sounds are often written with apostrophes or special marks that noisy text drops, so MT must treat the marked and stripped spellings as one word.

8A.question: Which 'l'-like (lateral) consonants the language has, if any.
8A.mt_relevance: Unusual lateral sounds (like Welsh 'll') get romanized as digraphs a tokenizer may split, and their rare letters raise the unknown-token rate.

9A.question: Whether the language has the 'ng' sound, and whether a word can begin with it.
9A.mt_relevance: Written as a digraph in many scripts, so MT can't always tell a word-initial 'ng' from a separate n-plus-g sequence.

10A.question: Whether the language uses nasal vowels — spoken through the nose — to tell words apart.
10A.mt_relevance: Nasal vowels ride on diacritics like 'ã' that casual text strips, collapsing a nasal word and its oral twin into one spelling.

10B.question: How many nasal-versus-oral vowel contrasts a language has, and whether nasality spreads.
10B.mt_relevance: Where nasal contrasts are dense and spread across a word, dropped nasal marks erase several distinctions at once — a recurring West African text issue.

11A.question: Whether the language has front rounded vowels, like German 'ü' or French 'eu'.
11A.mt_relevance: These vowels need umlaut letters (ü, ö) that ASCII-only text flattens to u or o, merging words the language keeps distinct.

12A.question: How complex a language's syllables can be, from simple ones to heavy consonant clusters.
12A.mt_relevance: Complex syllables pile up consonant clusters, so subword tokenizers split such words into many short pieces, lengthening sequences and straining alignment.

14A.question: Whether word stress always falls on a fixed syllable, like always the first or last.
14A.mt_relevance: Stress is almost never written, so this barely touches text MT; it matters mainly for speech translation and text-to-speech pronunciation.

15A.question: Whether stress depends on syllable weight, like vowel length or a closing consonant.
15A.mt_relevance: Syllable-weight stress leaves no mark in ordinary writing, so it bears on speech synthesis and pronunciation rather than translating text.

16A.question: What makes a syllable count as 'heavy' for stress — vowel length or a closing consonant.
16A.mt_relevance: This fine stress detail leaves no trace in spelling, informing pronunciation and speech models rather than text translation.

17A.question: Whether the language's rhythm puts stress at the start (trochaic) or end (iambic) of feet.
17A.mt_relevance: Purely a spoken-rhythm trait — it shapes speech synthesis and prosody, but has almost no effect on written text translation.

18A.question: Whether the language lacks consonants most languages have, like nasals or fricatives.
18A.mt_relevance: A phonological gap: it mostly changes how names and loanwords get spelled and transliterated, with little direct impact on text translation.

19A.question: Whether the language has rare consonants like clicks, pharyngeals or 'th' sounds.
19A.mt_relevance: Rare sounds often need special letters or digraphs, complicating transliteration and name handling more than sentence-level text translation.

21A.question: Whether one case ending marks only case, or fuses it with number, tense or other meanings.
21A.mt_relevance: Fused endings pack several grammatical meanings into one form, so MT must unpack them to align with languages that mark each separately.

21B.question: Whether a tense-aspect-mood ending also bundles in agreement, voice or polarity.
21B.mt_relevance: When one tense marker also encodes who acted or whether it's negated, MT must recover meanings the source packs into a single verb ending.

23A.question: Whether clause relations are marked on the verb (head) or on the nouns (dependents).
23A.mt_relevance: Head- vs dependent-marking changes where affixes attach, so MT must map object marking from a verb to a noun (or vice versa) across the pair.

24A.question: Whether possession is marked on the possessed noun (head) or the possessor (dependent).
24A.mt_relevance: In some languages the possessed thing takes the mark, in others the owner does — MT must relocate that mark to build a correct possessive.

25A.question: Whether a language marks grammar mostly on heads, on dependents, both, or neither overall.
25A.mt_relevance: A whole-language summary of where morphology lands — a broad signal of how much affix-shuffling a pair needs, not just one construction.

25B.question: Whether the subject and object of a verb carry no grammatical marking at all.
25B.mt_relevance: With neither argument marked, word order alone shows who did what, so MT leans on position and can misassign subject and object.

27A.question: Whether the language productively repeats whole or partial words to change meaning.
27A.mt_relevance: Doubling like 'buku-buku' for plurals maps one word to a phrase, and repeated tokens can trip up MT that treats repetition as an error.

28A.question: Whether different cases collapse into one shared form (case syncretism) or stay distinct.
28A.mt_relevance: When one ending covers several cases, the form is ambiguous and MT must use context to tell, say, subject from object apart.

29A.question: Whether a verb's agreement endings reuse one form across different persons or numbers.
29A.mt_relevance: Shared agreement endings blur which person or number is the subject, so MT may pick the wrong pronoun when translating outward.

32A.question: Whether nouns get their gender by meaning, by form, or the language has no gender.
32A.mt_relevance: How predictably gender is assigned tells MT whether it can infer a noun's gender from meaning or must memorize it word by word.

34A.question: Whether nouns mark plural, and if so whether it's optional or limited to humans.
34A.mt_relevance: When plural is optional or unmarked, MT must guess number from context to render languages like English that force singular vs plural.

35A.question: Whether plural pronouns like 'we' and 'they' use separate stems or added endings.
35A.mt_relevance: Number-indifferent pronouns leave 'we' vs 'I' unmarked, forcing MT to infer plurality from context to pick the right target pronoun.

36A.question: Whether the language has an 'and associates' plural, so 'John' can mean 'John's group'.
36A.mt_relevance: Associative plurals ('the Johns' = John's family) have no English word, so MT must unpack them into phrases like 'John and his people'.

39A.question: Whether 'we' has separate forms for 'we including you' versus 'we but not you'.
39A.mt_relevance: Translating into an inclusive/exclusive 'we' forces a choice English never marks: is the listener part of 'we' or not?

39B.question: Whether this Pama-Nyungan (Australian) language separates inclusive and exclusive 'we'.
39B.mt_relevance: The inclusive/exclusive 'we' split as found in Australian languages: MT into them must decide whether the addressee is inside 'we'.

40A.question: Whether the verb's 'we' agreement distinguishes 'including you' from 'excluding you'.
40A.mt_relevance: Here the inclusive/exclusive choice is baked into verb endings, so MT must resolve who is included even when no pronoun appears.

42A.question: Whether 'this' alone ('I want this') differs from 'this' before a noun ('this book').
42A.mt_relevance: If standalone and noun-modifying demonstratives use different forms, MT must pick the right one based on whether a noun follows.

43A.question: Whether third-person pronouns like 'he' or 'they' derive from demonstratives like 'that'.
43A.mt_relevance: Where 'he/she/it' come from 'this/that', pronouns can carry a near/far distance sense that nudges MT's choice of referring word.

44A.question: Whether pronouns mark gender (he vs she), and in which persons they do so.
44A.mt_relevance: Translating into gendered pronouns forces MT to guess he/she/it that a genderless-pronoun source like Turkish never specified.

46A.question: How 'someone' and 'something' are formed: from question words, generic nouns, or stems.
46A.mt_relevance: Interrogative-based indefinites reuse 'who/what' for 'someone/anyone', so MT must tell a question reading from an indefinite one.

47A.question: Whether emphatic 'himself' (the king himself) matches reflexive 'himself' (cut himself).
47A.mt_relevance: When emphasis and reflexive share one word (English 'himself'), MT must distinguish 'the king himself' from 'cut himself' to translate right.

48A.question: Whether prepositions carry person endings, like a single word for 'to-me' or 'with-us'.
48A.mt_relevance: Person-inflected adpositions fuse 'to me' into one word, so MT must build or split these forms with no separate pronoun to align.

50A.question: Whether case endings mark singular and plural evenly, or one number more than the other.
50A.mt_relevance: Uneven case-marking across number means MT can't reuse one ending pattern; it must track which number gets the extra or missing marker.

52A.question: Whether 'with a friend' (company) and 'with a knife' (tool) use the same marker.
52A.mt_relevance: English 'with' covers both company and instrument; MT into a language that splits them must decide which sense each phrase carries.

53A.question: How ordinals like 'first' and 'second' are formed, or if the language has them at all.
53A.mt_relevance: Irregular 'first/second' beside regular 'third, fourth' means MT can't just add an ending; suppletive ordinals must be learned per language.

54A.question: Whether the language marks distributive numerals like 'one each' or 'two apiece'.
54A.mt_relevance: A distributive form like 'two apiece' rarely has a one-word match, so MT must unpack it into a phrase or drop the 'each' entirely.

56A.question: Whether the word for 'and' looks like the word for 'all' or 'every'.
56A.mt_relevance: When 'and' and 'every' share a form, a system can misread coordination as quantification, confusing which nouns are listed versus totalled.

58A.question: Whether some nouns (like body parts or kin) must always be marked as possessed.
58A.mt_relevance: Into such a language, MT must invent a possessor — bare 'hand' has to become 'someone's hand', since unpossessed forms are ungrammatical.

58B.question: How many nouns the language requires to always appear possessed (none, one, a few, many).
58B.mt_relevance: The more such nouns, the more often MT into the language must supply a possessor the source left implicit.

59A.question: Whether the language sorts nouns into possession classes like alienable vs. inalienable.
59A.mt_relevance: Each class uses a different 'my/your' construction, so MT must know a noun's class before it can build the possessive phrase.

60A.question: Whether possessors, adjectives and relative clauses are marked alike or kept distinct.
60A.mt_relevance: When one marker covers possession, adjectives and relatives alike, MT must guess which modifier relation is meant before reordering it.

61A.question: Whether an adjective can stand alone without a noun, as in 'the poor'.
61A.mt_relevance: Into languages that require extra marking here, MT must nominalize a bare adjective — turning 'poor' into a proper 'the poor one' form.

62A.question: How the language turns a clause into a noun phrase, like 'the destruction of the city'.
62A.mt_relevance: Nominalizations often recode subject and object as possessors, so MT must recover who acted on whom before rendering it in the target.

63A.question: Whether the language uses the same word for 'and' and 'with'.
63A.mt_relevance: In 'with'-languages 'John and Mary' looks like 'John with Mary', so MT must decide whether it is coordination or an accompaniment phrase.

64A.question: Whether joining two nouns uses the same 'and' as joining two verbs or clauses.
64A.mt_relevance: If nouns and verbs take different connectives, MT must pick the right 'and' based on what it is joining, not reuse one word.

68A.question: Whether the language has a perfect form like 'has eaten', and where that form came from.
68A.mt_relevance: The perfect-vs-past line falls in different places across languages, so MT often picks the wrong one — 'I ate' vs 'I have eaten'.

71A.question: How the language forms a negative command like 'don't go!'.
71A.mt_relevance: A prohibitive may need a special verb form or negator, not just the imperative plus 'not', so MT must build the exact forbidding shape.

72A.question: How many persons the language can give commands to, from 'go!' to 'let's go'.
72A.mt_relevance: Systems differ in which persons take a command form, so MT must map English 'let's'/'let him' phrases onto (or out of) dedicated hortative inflections.

73A.question: Whether the language has a special verb form for wishes, like 'may you live long'.
73A.mt_relevance: A dedicated wish form has no single English match, so MT must render it with 'may...' or 'if only...' — and detect those when going the other way.

74A.question: How the language expresses situational possibility — being able to do something.
74A.mt_relevance: Whether ability is an affix or a separate word changes how many tokens carry 'can', complicating alignment and modal choice.

75A.question: How the language marks epistemic possibility — that something may or might be true.
75A.mt_relevance: Epistemic 'might/may' can be an affix or an auxiliary, and the target may force a certainty level the source left unstated.

76A.question: Whether a single marker covers both ability (situational) and likelihood (epistemic).
76A.mt_relevance: One marker for both readings is ambiguous — MT must decide if it means 'is able to' or 'is likely to' and can pick the wrong one.

79A.question: Whether verbs switch to a whole different stem across tenses or aspects (like go/went).
79A.mt_relevance: Suppletive stems like go→went share no letters, so a system must memorize them as whole forms rather than derive them by rule.

79B.question: Whether commands and 'let's' (hortative) forms use a completely different verb stem.
79B.mt_relevance: Irregular command and 'let's' stems can't be built from the base verb, so MT must learn each suppletive imperative on its own.

80A.question: Whether the verb changes form for how many participants or events (verbal number).
80A.mt_relevance: Some languages pick a different verb for one vs many participants — a distinction most source languages mark on the noun, not the verb.

81B.question: Which two basic subject-object-verb orders the language uses about equally.
81B.mt_relevance: With two competing basic orders, reordering into the target isn't fixed — MT must choose per sentence, raising the odds of a scrambled clause.

90B.question: Whether a relative clause ('that I bought') comes before the noun it describes.
90B.mt_relevance: A pre-noun relative clause must move to after the noun for English — a long reordering that easily drops or misattaches the clause.

90C.question: Whether a relative clause comes after the noun it describes, as in English.
90C.mt_relevance: Post-noun relative clauses match English order, so reordering is minimal — but relativizer choice and clause boundaries can still slip.

90D.question: Whether the modified noun sits inside its relative clause rather than outside it.
90D.mt_relevance: In internally-headed clauses the head noun is buried inside the clause, so MT must find it and lift it out for an external-head target.

90E.question: Whether the language uses correlative clauses — a paired 'which… that…' structure.
90E.mt_relevance: Correlative clauses pair a marker in one clause with a pronoun in the next — a structure English lacks and must fully recast.

90F.question: Whether relative clauses attach loosely at the sentence edge rather than being embedded.
90F.mt_relevance: Loosely adjoined clauses sit at the sentence margin with vague attachment, so MT must decide which noun each one modifies.

90G.question: Whether the modified noun appears twice — both inside and outside the relative clause.
90G.mt_relevance: A head noun repeated inside and outside the clause must collapse to one mention in English, or the output names the noun twice.

91A.question: Whether a degree word like 'very' comes before or after the adjective it modifies.
91A.mt_relevance: If 'very'-type words follow the adjective, MT must flip them to English's before-adjective order or produce phrases like 'tall very'.

94A.question: Where a word like 'because' or 'if' sits: before, after, or attached to its clause.
94A.mt_relevance: A clause-final or suffixed subordinator must be moved to the front as a word like 'because' when translating into English.

95A.question: Whether it uses prepositions or postpositions, and how that tracks object–verb order.
95A.mt_relevance: Postpositions put the 'to/from' after the noun, so both the adposition and often the verb must be repositioned for a prepositional VO language.

96A.question: Whether a describing clause (like 'that I saw') comes before or after its noun.
96A.mt_relevance: Prenominal relative clauses ('the I-saw book') must be unwound into a postnominal 'the book that I saw' — a heavy reordering for MT.

98A.question: How nouns get endings marking who acts and who is acted upon (case alignment).
98A.mt_relevance: Ergative systems mark a transitive subject like an object, so MT must re-map grammatical roles into English's subject/object frame.

99A.question: How pronouns change form to show who acts and who is acted upon (case alignment).
99A.mt_relevance: Pronoun case can follow a different alignment than nouns, so 'I/me' choices may not line up with how the source marks full nouns.

100A.question: How the verb's agreement endings treat the subject versus the object (alignment).
100A.mt_relevance: The verb can encode subject and object agreement on an ergative or hierarchical pattern English verbs lack, complicating agreement generation.

101A.question: Whether subject pronouns are separate words, verb endings, or often left unsaid.
101A.mt_relevance: Pro-drop or affix-only subjects mean the source may omit 'I/you/he', which MT must recover and insert as an explicit pronoun in English.

102A.question: Whether the verb agrees with its subject, its object, both, or neither.
102A.mt_relevance: Verbs that agree with both subject and object pack role information English spreads across separate words, so that alignment can be lost.

103A.question: Whether 'he/she/it' subject agreement on the verb is shown by no marking at all.
103A.mt_relevance: A bare, unmarked third-person form can look like an uninflected stem, making it harder for MT to tell 'he goes' from a citation form.

104A.question: When a verb carries both subject and object markers, which one comes first.
104A.mt_relevance: Affix order matters mainly when generating verb forms for agreement-rich targets; it rarely changes word order in the output sentence.

105A.question: How the language frames 'give X to Y' — the recipient versus the thing given.
105A.mt_relevance: Double-object vs. to-dative framing ('give her it' vs. 'give it to her') forces MT to pick a construction the source may not signal.

106A.question: Whether 'each other' is expressed differently from 'themselves' (reflexive).
106A.mt_relevance: When one form covers both 'each other' and 'themselves', MT must disambiguate a reciprocal from a reflexive reading the source leaves merged.

107A.question: Whether the language has a passive voice (like 'the door was opened').
107A.mt_relevance: A language with no passive must recast 'was opened' as an active clause, adding or reordering an agent MT has to supply.

108A.question: Whether the object can be demoted or dropped with a special 'antipassive' form.
108A.mt_relevance: Antipassives sideline or drop the object in ergative languages — a voice English lacks — so MT must map them onto objectless or generic-object clauses.

108B.question: How productively the language forms antipassives that drop the verb's object.
108B.mt_relevance: A productive antipassive drops objects across many verbs, so MT often meets objectless clauses whose suppressed object must be recovered in a language that states it.

109A.question: Whether the language can promote an extra role, like a beneficiary, to direct object.
109A.mt_relevance: Applicatives fold a 'for/with/at' phrase into the verb, so MT must add or remove a preposition when translating either way.

109B.question: Which extra roles — beneficiary, instrument, location — the language can make an object.
109B.mt_relevance: The role an applied object carries — instrument vs location — tells MT which hidden preposition, 'with' or 'at', to spell out.

110A.question: Whether the language uses a separate verb to say 'make someone do something'.
110A.mt_relevance: A causative built from a helper verb may map to one causative-marked word in the target, forcing MT to fuse two verbs into one.

111A.question: Whether the language marks causing with an affix or compound rather than a helper verb.
111A.mt_relevance: A one-word causative verb often lacks a single-word target equivalent, so MT must unpack it into a 'make someone do…' phrase.

113A.question: Whether making a sentence negative just adds a word or also reshapes the verb.
113A.mt_relevance: If negation reshapes the verb instead of just adding 'not', MT must rebuild the verb form, not merely insert a negator.

114A.question: Which verb category negation alters — its finiteness (full vs. reduced form) or another.
114A.mt_relevance: Knowing which category flips under negation tells MT which verb morphology — mood or finiteness — to change to produce a negative.

115A.question: Whether 'nobody/nothing' still needs a negative verb (double negation) or stands alone.
115A.mt_relevance: Some languages require a second negative on the verb with 'nobody'; MT into single-negation languages must not emit a wrong double negative.

117A.question: How the language says someone owns something — with a 'have' verb or another way.
117A.mt_relevance: Languages without a 'have' verb say 'to-me is a book', so MT must restructure the clause rather than translate 'have' directly.

118A.question: Whether an adjective in 'it is big' acts like a verb or needs a linking 'to be'.
118A.mt_relevance: Verb-like adjectives carry tense and need no 'to be', so MT must insert or delete a copula when translating them.

119A.question: Whether 'she is a teacher' and 'she is at home' use the same linking construction.
119A.mt_relevance: Some languages use different copulas for identity vs location, like Spanish ser/estar, so MT must pick the correct one.

120A.question: Whether the language can drop the linking verb in 'she (is) a doctor'.
120A.mt_relevance: From a copula-dropping language MT must supply 'is/are'; into one it should delete the copula to sound natural.

121A.question: How the language says one thing exceeds another, as in 'taller than X'.
121A.mt_relevance: 'Than' has no counterpart in exceed-type ('tall surpasses X') or conjoined ('this tall, that short') comparisons, so MT must recast them.

122A.question: How the language builds relative clauses like 'the man who left', on the subject.
122A.mt_relevance: Some languages leave a gap in the subject slot while others keep a resumptive pronoun ('the man that he left'), so MT must insert or delete it.

123A.question: How the language forms relative clauses on oblique roles (e.g. 'the man I gave it to').
123A.mt_relevance: Relativizing an oblique like 'the house I live in' may need a resumptive pronoun in one language but a gap in another — MT must insert or delete it.

124A.question: Whether 'want' phrases leave the subject implicit ('want to go') or state it overtly.
124A.mt_relevance: Translating into a language that restates the subject, MT must supply a pronoun the source's 'want to go' construction left unspoken.

125A.question: Whether purpose clauses ('in order to…') use a full finite verb or a reduced verb form.
125A.mt_relevance: Deranked purpose verbs (infinitives or special forms) must be expanded into or collapsed from full 'so that' clauses across languages.

126A.question: Whether 'when' time clauses use a full finite verb or a reduced (non-finite) verb form.
126A.mt_relevance: A deranked 'when' verb often drops tense and subject marking, which MT must reconstruct when the target language wants a full clause.

127A.question: Whether reason clauses ('because…') use a full finite verb or a reduced verb form.
127A.mt_relevance: Reduced reason clauses can blur cause and purpose, so MT risks translating 'because' as 'in order to' or vice versa.

128A.question: Whether 'say/tell' complement clauses use a full finite verb or a reduced verb form.
128A.mt_relevance: Reported speech shifts: a finite 'that…' complement needs a complementizer plus tense and pronoun changes a deranked source verb doesn't carry.

130A.question: Whether one word means both 'hand' and 'finger' or the two have separate words.
130A.mt_relevance: A single word for both 'hand' and 'finger' forces MT to pick the right one from context; mostly a word-choice, not structural, issue.

130B.question: Whether speakers who merge 'hand' and 'finger' are foragers, mixed, or full farmers.
130B.mt_relevance: This is ethnographic metadata about subsistence economy, not a grammatical trait — effectively no impact on text translation.

131A.question: What base the counting system uses — decimal (10), vigesimal (20), or body-part.
131A.mt_relevance: Non-decimal or restricted number systems may lack words for large or exact numbers, forcing MT to paraphrase or fall back on digits.

132A.question: How many basic, non-derived colour words the language has, from 3 up to 5.5.
132A.mt_relevance: With only a few basic colour words, one term spans several hues, so MT must guess the exact shade a target language names on its own.

133A.question: How many basic colour categories the language names in total, from 3-4 up to 9-10.
133A.mt_relevance: Colour vocabularies split unevenly, so a hue named in the source may have no single word in the target, forcing a descriptive paraphrase.

134A.question: Whether the language separates 'green' and 'blue' or merges them into one 'grue' term.
134A.mt_relevance: A single 'grue' word can't be cleanly split into 'green' or 'blue' when translating out, so MT must guess which the writer meant.

135A.question: Whether the language separates 'red' and 'yellow' or covers both with one word.
135A.mt_relevance: When one term covers both red and yellow, MT into a colour-splitting language must choose one and can pick the wrong shade.

136B.question: Whether the word for 'I/me' contains an 'm' sound, as in English 'me' and 'my'.
136B.mt_relevance: This is a historical sound pattern in the pronoun, not a grammar rule — essentially no effect on text translation quality.

137A.question: Whether first-person pronouns use an 'n' sound and second-person an 'm' sound.
137A.mt_relevance: A historical sound pattern in pronoun forms; essentially no effect on how a text-translation system handles pronouns as whole words.

137B.question: Whether the word for singular 'you' contains an 'm' sound.
137B.mt_relevance: A lexical sound trait of a single pronoun; negligible impact on text translation, which treats each pronoun as one token.

139A.question: How many negation signs are irregular rather than regularly formed, in a sign language.
139A.mt_relevance: Sign languages lack a standard written form, so this concerns sign-language (video) translation, not text MT.

140A.question: How many separate question particles (question-marking signs) a sign language has.
140A.mt_relevance: Concerns manual question-marking signs; relevant to sign-language translation, not written text MT.

141A.question: What kind of writing system the language uses (alphabet, syllabary, logographic, etc.).
141A.mt_relevance: Script type drives tokenization: logographic scripts run words together with no spaces, while consonantal scripts omit vowels — both strain MT tokenizers.

142A.question: Whether click sounds are used to signal meanings like 'yes', 'no', or disapproval.
142A.mt_relevance: Paralinguistic clicks (like English 'tsk') are seldom written down, so this has little effect on text translation.

143B.question: Whether negating a clause requires two negative words (like French ne…pas).
143B.mt_relevance: Obligatory double negation forces MT to insert both negators; dropping either yields ungrammatical or wrongly-affirmative output.

143C.question: Whether a clause can optionally take a second negative word alongside the main negator.
143C.mt_relevance: Optional second negators vary by register and dialect; MT must decide whether to add one, risking over- or under-marked negation.

143D.question: Whether negation can optionally be marked with three negative elements in one clause.
143D.mt_relevance: A rare three-way negation option MT seldom needs to produce, but it must not read stacked negators as cancelling each other out.

143E.question: Whether negation is marked before the verb, as a separate word or a prefix.
143E.mt_relevance: Preverbal negators sit where many languages place none; MT must put the negator on the correct side of the verb to keep the clause negative.

143F.question: Whether negation is marked after the verb, as a separate word or a suffix.
143F.mt_relevance: Postverbal negation (like a negative suffix) trails the verb; MT must attach it correctly or the negation lands on the wrong word.

143G.question: Whether negation is shown by tone change, an infix, or a change in the verb stem.
143G.mt_relevance: Negation carried by tone or a stem change leaves little visible trace in plain text, so MT can miss the negation entirely.

144B.question: Where the negative word sits in the clause — near the verb, or at its start or end.
144B.mt_relevance: Free-standing negators can drift far from the verb; MT must place them where the target grammar expects, not mirror the source position.

144C.question: Whether the basic word order changes when a clause is made negative.
144C.mt_relevance: Some languages reorder subject, object and verb only in negatives; MT must apply that shift instead of copying the affirmative order.

144D.question: Where the negative marker goes in a subject-verb-object (SVO) sentence.
144D.mt_relevance: MT must drop 'not' into the exact slot the target uses — before or after the verb — or the negation reads as ungrammatical or shifts scope.

144E.question: Whether an SVO (subject-verb-object) language has more than one way to say 'not'.
144E.mt_relevance: Several competing negation patterns mean MT must pick the one that fits the tense, clause type or register, not just any grammatical option.

144F.question: Whether an SVO (subject-verb-object) language needs two negative words, not one.
144F.mt_relevance: Two negators must both be produced and placed (as with French 'ne…pas'); emitting only one leaves the clause half-negated or wrong.

144G.question: Whether an SVO (subject-verb-object) language can add an optional second negative word.
144G.mt_relevance: When translating INTO this language, MT may add or omit the optional second negator, but must never leave the one required marker out.

144H.question: Whether a sentence-initial negative word (in SVO order) also needs a second negative.
144H.mt_relevance: A clause-opening negator sits far from the verb it negates; MT must carry that long-distance scope and add any required paired negative.

144I.question: Whether a negative just before the verb is a separate word or a prefix on it.
144I.mt_relevance: A prefix negator fuses into one verb token; a separate word doesn't — MT must attach or detach 'not' to match the target's word-building.

144J.question: Whether a negative right after the verb is a separate word or a suffix on it.
144J.mt_relevance: A suffixed negator glues onto the verb's end; MT generating this language must inflect the verb rather than insert a free-standing 'not'.

144K.question: Whether a sentence-final negative word can stand alone or needs a second negative.
144K.mt_relevance: A sentence-final negator surfaces only at the very end, so MT must hold negation back to the last position instead of marking it early.

144L.question: Where the negative marker goes in a subject-object-verb (SOV) sentence.
144L.mt_relevance: Verb-final languages usually park the negator at the clause end near the verb; MT must move 'not' there from a verb-medial source sentence.

144M.question: Whether an SOV (subject-object-verb) language has more than one way to say 'not'.
144M.mt_relevance: Choosing among a verb-final language's several negation frames is an extra decision MT resolves from context, not by defaulting to the commonest one.

144N.question: Whether an SOV (subject-object-verb) language needs two negative words, not one.
144N.mt_relevance: Both mandatory negators must be generated and slotted around the clause-final verb; producing just one yields incomplete, ungrammatical negation.

144O.question: Whether an SOV (subject-object-verb) language can add an optional second negative word.
144O.mt_relevance: Reading FROM such a language, a lone negator can still be a full negation — MT must not mistake a missing optional second marker for affirmation.

144P.question: Whether a sentence-initial negative word (in SOV order) also needs a second negative.
144P.mt_relevance: In verb-final order the negator leads but the verb trails, so MT keeps negation scoped across the whole clause and adds any paired negative.

144Q.question: Whether a negative between the subject and object needs a second negative word.
144Q.mt_relevance: This negator lands early, ahead of object and verb; MT must slot it right after the subject and add a partner negative where the language needs one.

144R.question: In verb-final (SOV) languages, whether the pre-verb negative is a word or a prefix.
144R.mt_relevance: MT must get this preverbal negator's slot and word-vs-prefix form right; misplacing or dropping it can flip the clause to its opposite meaning.

144S.question: In verb-final (SOV) languages, whether the negative follows the verb as a word or suffix.
144S.mt_relevance: A post-verb or suffixed negative sits apart from what it denies, so MT must carry negation scope across the whole clause or lose the 'not'.

144T.question: In verb-first languages, where the negative sits relative to verb, subject and object.
144T.mt_relevance: Verb-initial languages park the negative before, inside, or after the verb complex, so MT must learn which slot each one uses to avoid mis-scoping.

144U.question: In verb-first languages, whether negation uses two markers (double negation) per clause.
144U.mt_relevance: Languages that require two negative markers per clause tempt MT to emit only one, leaving a half-negated, ungrammatical sentence.

144V.question: In verb-first languages, whether a negative appears before the verb as a word or prefix.
144V.mt_relevance: A preverbal negative in a verb-first clause must land ahead of the verb; misplacing it makes MT deny the wrong part of the sentence.

144W.question: In verb-first languages, whether the negative comes just after the verb or mid-clause.
144W.mt_relevance: A negative wedged just after the verb or between subject and object is easy for MT to drop or shift, silently reversing the meaning.

144X.question: In verb-first languages, whether the negative word comes at the very end of the clause.
144X.mt_relevance: A clause-final negative can sit many words from the verb, so MT must hold the negation open to the sentence's end or it never appears.

144Y.question: In object-first languages, where the negative sits relative to verb and subject.
144Y.mt_relevance: Object-first order is rare in training data, so MT frequently mishandles where these languages place the negative and flips polarity.
